draft.change: Broaden the definition of the existing “toward (turning, looking)” sense in elah to include directing attention, and add Genesis 4:5 as evidence.
draft.definition: With a verb of turning, looking, or paying heed, אֶל marks the person or thing toward which attention is directed.
draft.evidence: Genesis 4:5 puts אֶל קַיִן before לֹא שָׁעָה. Cain is the object of Yahweh’s regard in the negated clause, just as Abel is in the affirmative clause in Genesis 4:4.

patch.value: Marks the person or thing toward which someone turns or directs attention, including one looked to for help or worship.
The first אֶל in וְאֶל קַיִן introduces Cain as the person to whom Yahweh paid no heed. The second introduces his offering.
“Turn to me and be saved, all the ends of the earth.”
Whoever was bitten and looked to the bronze serpent lived.
“They looked to him and were radiant.”

analysis.evidence: In וְאֶל קַיִן וְאֶל מִנְחָתוֹ לֹא שָׁעָה, the first אֶל introduces Cain as the person to whom Yahweh paid no heed. The repeated אֶל introduces his offering alongside him. The negation לֹא applies to שָׁעָה.
analysis.morphology: Prefixed conjunction וְ, here adversative (“but”), followed by the preposition אֶל governing קַיִן. No pronominal suffix.
analysis.sense: Marks the person toward whom attention is directed.

draft.change: Add a personal-name article for Cain with its etymology left open pending evidence.
draft.definition: Cain, the son of Adam and Eve and brother of Abel.
draft.evidence: Genesis 4:1 names Eve’s son קַיִן. Genesis 4:2 identifies Abel as his brother and names Cain again when describing his work.

analysis.evidence: The repeated וְאֶל pairs קַיִן with מִנְחָתוֹ (“his offering”). Cain is the person to whom שָׁעָה לֹא applies alongside his offering.
analysis.morphology: Masculine singular proper noun, governed by the preceding וְאֶל, with no attached prefix or suffix.
analysis.sense: The personal name of Abel’s brother.

analysis.evidence: The repeated וְאֶל pairs Cain with his offering as the two objects of God’s regard in לֹא שָׁעָה. The suffix ־וֹ refers to Cain.
analysis.morphology: Feminine singular noun in the construct state with a third-person masculine singular possessive suffix ־וֹ.

analysis.evidence: לֹא directly precedes the perfect verb שָׁעָה. Together they state that the LORD did not look with favor on Cain and his offering.
analysis.morphology: Negative particle without prefix or suffix.

analysis.evidence: The two אֶל phrases identify Cain and his offering as the objects of regard. לֹא negates שָׁעָה, so the clause says that YHWH had no regard for Cain or his offering, reversing the preceding verse’s statement about Abel and his offering.
analysis.morphology: Qal perfect, third person masculine singular, with no prefix or suffix.

analysis.evidence: In וַיִּחַר לְקַיִן מְאֹד, the verb is used impersonally. לְקַיִן identifies Cain as the one who feels the anger, and מְאֹד marks its intensity. The following clause says that his face fell.
analysis.morphology: Qal wayyiqtol, third masculine singular, with prefixed וַ־ and an apocopated verb form.

draft.change: Add a personal-name article for Cain with its etymology left open pending evidence.
draft.definition: Cain, the son of Adam and Eve and brother of Abel.
draft.evidence: Genesis 4:1 names Eve’s son קַיִן. Genesis 4:2 identifies Abel as his brother and names Cain again when describing his work.

analysis.evidence: In וַיִּחַר לְקַיִן מְאֹד, לְ marks Cain as the person experiencing anger. The clause means “Cain became very angry.” He is the same Cain named earlier in the verse alongside his offering.
analysis.morphology: Preposition לְ prefixed to the masculine singular personal name קַיִן.
analysis.sense: The personal name of Abel’s brother.

analysis.evidence: In וַיִּחַר לְקַיִן מְאֹד (“Cain became very angry”), מְאֹד intensifies וַיִּחַר, expressing the degree of Cain’s anger.
analysis.morphology: Adverb of degree, with no prefix or suffix.

analysis.evidence: The plural verb agrees with פָּנָיו, “his face,” which is plural in Hebrew. After וַיִּחַר לְקַיִן מְאֹד, “Cain was very angry,” the phrase describes the visible change in his expression.
analysis.morphology: Qal wayyiqtol, third person masculine plural, with prefixed וַ־.

analysis.evidence: After the verse says that Cain grew very angry, וַיִּפְּלוּ פָּנָיו describes the visible change in his expression: his face fell. The plural verb וַיִּפְּלוּ agrees with פָּנָיו, which denotes one person’s countenance.
analysis.morphology: Common-gender plural noun in construct with a third-person masculine singular possessive suffix referring to Cain.
